title: What is your Git branching strategy (GitFlow, trunk-based, feature branches), and why maintain separate `production` and `development` branches instead of a single branch with tags?
shortTitle: Git branching strategy (GitFlow, trunk-based, feature branches) and why maintain separate production and development branches instead of a single branch with tags

s1_definition.profdef: A branching strategy is the agreed convention for how a team uses branches to develop, integrate, release, and hotfix code. GitFlow uses long-lived develop and main branches plus feature, release, and hotfix branches, suiting scheduled releases. Trunk-based development keeps everyone committing to a single main branch with very short-lived feature branches merged daily behind feature flags, suiting continuous delivery. Maintaining separate production and development branches gives you a stable, always-deployable line representing exactly what is in production and a separate integration line for in-progress work, so you can hotfix production independently of unreleased changes — something a single branch with tags makes clumsy because tags are immutable points, not a branch you can commit fixes onto.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India keeps two sets of operating procedures. One binder, the production binder, contains only the exact procedures currently running in every branch where Rajesh and Priya bank — it is sacred and always correct. The other binder, the development binder, is where new procedures are drafted, tested, and refined before they are approved. You keep them separate because if a dangerous bug is found in the live procedures, you must fix the production binder immediately and push that fix to all branches, without accidentally also shipping half-finished draft procedures. A single binder with sticky notes marking old versions does not let you safely make a new correction on top of a past version.
s1_definition.oneliner: Pick GitFlow for scheduled releases, trunk-based for continuous delivery, and keep production and development as separate branches so you can hotfix live code independently of unreleased work — which tags on a single branch cannot do.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A branching strategy is the agreed convention for how a team uses branches to develop, integrate, release, and hotfix code. GitFlow uses long-lived develop and main branches plus feature, release, and hotfix branches, suiting scheduled releases. Trunk-based development keeps everyone committing to a single main branch with very short-lived feature branches merged daily behind feature flags, suiting continuous delivery. Maintaining separate production and development branches gives you a stable, always-deployable line representing exactly what is in production and a separate integration line for in-progress work, so you can hotfix production independently of unreleased changes — something a single branch with tags makes clumsy because tags are immutable points, not a branch you can commit fixes onto.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India keeps two sets of operating procedures. One binder, the production binder, contains only the exact procedures currently running in every branch where Rajesh and Priya bank — it is sacred and always correct. The other binder, the development binder, is where new procedures are drafted, tested, and refined before they are approved. You keep them separate because if a dangerous bug is found in the live procedures, you must fix the production binder immediately and push that fix to all branches, without accidentally also shipping half-finished draft procedures. A single binder with sticky notes marking old versions does not let you safely make a new correction on top of a past version.

**One line to remember:** Pick GitFlow for scheduled releases, trunk-based for continuous delivery, and keep production and development as separate branches so you can hotfix live code independently of unreleased work — which tags on a single branch cannot do.

sections.s2_technical:
GitFlow is the most structured model. It has two permanent branches: main, which always reflects production-released code, and develop, the integration branch for the next release. Work happens on feature branches cut from develop and merged back when complete. When a release is prepared, a release branch is cut from develop for final stabilisation, then merged into both main and develop, and main is tagged with the version. Urgent production fixes use a hotfix branch cut from main, merged back into both main and develop so the fix is not lost. GitFlow suits teams with scheduled, versioned releases and multiple versions in support, but it is heavy — many branches and merges — and it slows continuous delivery.

Trunk-based development is the opposite philosophy, favoured for continuous delivery and most modern web services. Everyone integrates into a single trunk, main, at least daily. Feature branches are tiny and live hours, not weeks, so you avoid the painful big-bang merges and long-lived divergence that plague GitFlow. Incomplete features are hidden behind feature flags so trunk is always releasable even with half-built features present. Trunk-based requires strong automated testing and CI because everyone shares one line, but it maximises integration frequency, which is the single biggest predictor of healthy delivery. Releases are cut from trunk, sometimes via short-lived release branches for stabilisation.

Feature-branch workflow is the common middle ground, often called GitHub Flow in its simplest form: main is always deployable, and every change is a feature branch opened as a pull request, reviewed, passed through CI, and merged to main, which is then deployed. It is simpler than GitFlow and close to trunk-based with slightly longer-lived branches. Which model a team picks depends on release cadence, the need to support multiple versions, team size, and CI maturity.

The specific question of separate production and development branches versus a single branch with tags is about operational capability. A production branch is a living line of development: it has a HEAD you can commit onto, so when a critical bug hits live, you branch a hotfix from production, fix it, deploy, and merge the fix back — all while the development branch continues to hold unreleased work you are not ready to ship. A tag, by contrast, is an immutable pointer to one commit; it marks "this is what we released" but you cannot commit onto a tag. If you only had a single branch with tags and production was several commits behind the branch HEAD, you could not simply add a fix on top of the released state without either dragging in the unreleased commits or doing awkward surgery. The two-branch model cleanly separates "what is live and must stay stable" from "what we are building," which is exactly what lets you hotfix safely and keep an audit trail of what was deployed. A senior nuance: the branching model must match your deployment model — if you truly deploy trunk continuously, you may not need a separate production branch at all because trunk IS production and tags suffice; the separate-branch argument is strongest when there is a real gap between what is released and what is in development, which is common in banking where releases are gated by compliance and change windows.
sections.s3_banking:
The National Bank of India releases its transfer service on a controlled schedule due to compliance change windows, so it keeps a production branch and a development branch. A critical bug is found in production while unreleased features sit on development.

Problem 1 — The team develops a new feature on a feature branch cut from development and merges it back; development now holds unreleased work that is not yet approved for the live environment.

Problem 2 — A critical bug is discovered in production where transfers for Rajesh and Priya are miscalculating fees. The team must hotfix production immediately without shipping the unreleased development work. A production branch allows a hotfix branch to be cut from the exact live state.

Problem 3 — After the hotfix is deployed to production, it must be merged back into development so the fix is not lost when development is eventually released. This back-merge is why the two-branch model is clean.

Our runnable Java simulation models a tiny branch graph: a `Branch` with commits, a `Repo` that supports branching, committing, hotfixing, and merging, and a demo that shows a hotfix applied to production and back-merged to development while unreleased commits stay unshipped. Classes: `Commit`, `Branch`, `Repo`, and a `BranchingDemo` main.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -cp target/classes com.bank.vcs.BranchingDemo

# Real GitFlow-style hotfix on separate prod/dev branches:
git checkout production
git checkout -b hotfix/fee-calc            # cut hotfix from the LIVE state
# ... make the fix ...
git commit -am "fix fee calculation (BigDecimal rounding)"
git checkout production && git merge --no-ff hotfix/fee-calc   # deploy to prod
git tag -a v1.0.1 -m "hotfix fee calc"
git checkout development && git merge --no-ff hotfix/fee-calc  # back-merge so fix is not lost
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: a repository with a production branch holding the live transfer service and a development branch holding unreleased work, plus a new feature and a critical live bug.

Step 1: The production branch is created with the single live commit for the transfer service v1.0. This branch represents exactly what is running where Rajesh and Priya bank, and it must stay stable.

Step 2: The development branch is created from production, so it starts identical. A short-lived feature branch for UPI transfers is cut from development, a commit is added, and it is merged back into development. Development now contains the unreleased UPI work, which is not yet approved for the live environment.

Step 3: A critical bug is found in production — transfer fees are miscalculated. Because production is a real branch with a committable HEAD, a hotfix branch is cut from the exact live production state, not from development, so the hotfix carries none of the unreleased UPI work.

Step 4: The hotfix commit is made and the hotfix branch is merged into production, deploying the fee fix to the live environment. Crucially, the unreleased UPI feature stays out of production, exactly as intended, because the hotfix came from production, not development.

Step 5: The hotfix is then back-merged into development so the fix is not lost when development is eventually released. The final checks prove the separation: production does not have the UPI feature, production has the fee fix, and development also has the fee fix. This is precisely the capability a single branch with immutable tags cannot provide cleanly.

sections.s6_takeaway:
My branching strategy depends on the team's release model. GitFlow is the structured model with permanent main and develop branches plus feature, release, and hotfix branches; it suits scheduled, versioned releases and supporting multiple versions, but it is heavy with many merges and it slows continuous delivery. Trunk-based development is the opposite: everyone integrates into a single trunk at least daily, feature branches live hours not weeks, and incomplete work hides behind feature flags so trunk is always releasable. It needs strong CI and automated tests, but it maximises integration frequency, which is the biggest predictor of healthy delivery. The feature-branch or GitHub Flow model is the common middle ground, where main is always deployable and every change is a reviewed pull request.

On the specific question of separate production and development branches versus a single branch with tags, the answer is about operational capability. A production branch is a living line of development with a committable HEAD, so when a critical bug hits the live system I can branch a hotfix from the exact production state, fix it, deploy, and merge the fix back, all while the development branch continues to hold unreleased work I am not ready to ship. A tag is only an immutable pointer to one commit; it records what was released but you cannot commit onto a tag. If I had a single branch with tags and production was several commits behind the branch HEAD, I could not cleanly add a fix on top of the released state without dragging in unreleased commits or doing awkward surgery.

In my project at the National Bank of India, releases were gated by compliance change windows, so we kept a production branch and a development branch. One day a critical bug miscalculated transfer fees for live customers like Rajesh and Priya while an unreleased UPI feature sat on development. Because production was a real branch, I cut a hotfix from the exact live state, fixed the rounding, and merged it straight to production, deploying the fix without shipping the unapproved UPI work, and then I back-merged the hotfix into development so it would not be lost at the next release. That clean separation of what is live and must stay stable from what we are building is exactly what the two-branch model gives you and what immutable tags on a single branch cannot. The nuance I always add is that the model must match the deployment reality — if you truly deploy trunk continuously, trunk is production and tags may suffice, but whenever there is a real gap between what is released and what is in development, separate branches are what let you hotfix safely and keep a clear audit trail.
